facts.text: The opening narration is by Vic Perrin, uncredited. He was also "The Control Voice" of The Outer Limits, and he voices the lead gargoyle here too.
Director Bill L. Norton came to Gargoyles after his debut feature Cisco Pike (1971). He later directed More American Graffiti (1979) and episodes of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel.
Gargoyles was the first film job for makeup artist Stan Winston, fresh out of Disney's apprenticeship. He later won four Oscars for Aliens, Jurassic Park and Terminator 2.
Winston threatened to quit unless makeup artists got screen credit. He got it, and the credit let him share the 1973 Emmy for Outstanding Achievement in Makeup.
Winston sculpted the background gargoyle masks at his dining room table in two weeks. His wife Karen rolled the clay balls that became the scales.
Goof: in this car ride to Uncle Willie's, the knee of a sound man is visible in the back seat behind Dr. Boley (Cornel Wilde).
The whole movie was shot with a single camera in just 18 days. A previous director reportedly turned the job down as impossible, so Bill L. Norton stepped in.
Temperatures in Carlsbad, New Mexico often topped 100°F (38°C) during the shoot, while the gargoyle actors wore neoprene wetsuits covered in fishnet and rubber bits.
Grayson Hall (Mrs. Parks, and Dark Shadows' Dr. Julia Hoffman) came up with the idea of holding a drink in every scene she appears in.
Grayson Hall's husband, Sam Hall, became a Dark Shadows writer after producer Dan Curtis met him at a party at the couple's home. She was already on the show at the time.
Grayson Hall was Oscar-nominated for The Night of the Iguana (1964). On Dark Shadows she was meant to be killed off within weeks, but was so good she stayed for the whole run.
Bernie Casey, the lead gargoyle, played for the 49ers and Rams. He was also a serious painter with a fine arts master's, and Stan Winston owned several of his paintings.
Casey's own voice was swapped out in post-production. It didn't suit the head gargoyle, so Vic Perrin dubbed him.
Goof: as the shed collapses on Uncle Willie, a crew member or the director gets knocked down in the lower right corner and scrambles out of frame.
The burned-out building was a real abandoned motel, the Cactus Motel on US 62 near Carlsbad, NM. Its ruins were later registered as an archaeological site with the state.
Goof: as the Boleys flee in the station wagon, a gargoyle smashes the driver's window, yet the gargoyle beside the headlights vanishes when they back up.
The gargoyle action was slowed down on purpose to give the creatures an unnatural, jerky look. One reviewer called it "arty jerky-slow-motion photography."
One reviewer figured most of the budget went into the monsters: the gargoyle costumes get plenty of screen time, while the script, direction and acting got short shrift.
Jennifer Salt (Diana Boley) is the daughter of Midnight Cowboy screenwriter Waldo Salt, and she played Crazy Annie in that film. She later produced American Horror Story.
Salt reunited with director Brian De Palma the same year for Sisters (1972). She also roomed with Margot Kidder and partied with young Spielberg and Scorsese.
Star Cornel Wilde (Dr. Mercer Boley) was on the 1936 U.S. Olympic fencing team and was Oscar-nominated for playing Chopin in A Song to Remember (1945).
Wilde directed as well as acted, including the survival classic The Naked Prey (1965). Gargoyles was the only made-for-TV movie he ever starred in.
Gargoyles was produced by Tomorrow Entertainment for CBS, with Roger Gimbel as executive producer. Cinematographer Earl Rath shot it around Carlsbad, Carlsbad Caverns and Laredo, Texas.
Wilde spoke six languages, and his role as Tybalt in a 1940 Broadway Romeo and Juliet with Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh led to his Warner Bros. contract.
Scott Glenn plays biker James Reeger. He went on to The Right Stuff, Silence of the Lambs and The Hunt for Red October, and was a Kenosha, Wisconsin newspaper reporter before acting.
Screenwriters Stephen and Elinor Karpf also wrote the TV movie The Jayne Mansfield Story and the horror film Devil Dog: The Hound from Hell, so killer creatures were a recurring theme.
Goof: around here the cameraman's shadow falls across a tree.
Winston wasn't even supposed to apply the lead gargoyle makeup. He got that job because of friction between Bernie Casey and designer Ellis "Sonny" Burman Jr.
Sonny Burman, who designed the lead gargoyle, was the son of a monster-mask sculptor who worked on Universal's Frankenstein and Wolf Man films. He later won an Emmy for Star Trek: DS9.
Vic Perrin, the gargoyle leader's voice, also voiced the Metron in Star Trek's 'Arena' and Nomad in 'The Changeling', and uncredited narrated Spartacus (1960) and One Million Years B.C.
Many cars are listed in the continuity goofs: the cops' car chasing the dirt bikes flips between a Chevy Impala and a Ford LTD.
Bernie Casey, the lead gargoyle, later became the first Black actor to play James Bond's CIA ally Felix Leiter, in Never Say Never Again (1983).
Uncle Willie says the Native American name for the creatures is "nakatekachinko", and the dance that summons them is "nonataya".
A stuntman who plays one of the bikers also suited up as one of the gargoyles.
Before Gargoyles, Stan Winston was working in Disney's mailroom. His mentor Bob Schiffer recommended him to makeup supervisor Del Armstrong, and that call landed his first professional job.
A reviewer noted the lead gargoyle gets increasingly interested in the human Diana, calling it "interspecies erotica", which is unusual for early-70s network TV.
Gargoyles aired on CBS on November 21, 1972. It was written by Stephen and Elinor Karpf and repeated on the CBS Late Movie in 1973 and twice in 1975.
Winston later called the Gargoyles credit pushback part of his ego: he asked for a title card again on The Bat People (1974). He said it helped raise the status of makeup artists.
Winston said he was embarrassed when the DVD cover billed it as a "Stan Winston" film. He felt Sonny Burman and makeup supervisor Del Armstrong deserved more credit.
Actor William Stevens, the police chief here, is also known for playing Officer Jerry Walters on the TV series Adam-12.
Gargoyles is name-checked in the horror film Jeepers Creepers (2001), and in Stan Winston tribute documentaries.
Of the ten actors billed in the end titles, five die in the film.
The DVD runs 74 minutes: the European theatrical cut, slightly longer than the original US TV broadcast.
Vic Perrin also voiced Dr. Zin in Jonny Quest and the original narration of Epcot's Spaceship Earth.
The rolling end credits include "Creators of Gargoyle Make-Up: Ellis Burman & Stan Winston," the credit Winston fought for.
Goof: a cable can be seen holding up a gargoyle as it flies in the finale.
